newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Winnie Mandela faces contest in ANC Women's League.
newsitem.headline: Winnie Mandela faces contest in ANC Women's League.

text.p: Winnie Madikizela-Mandela, fallen heroine of South Africa's apartheid struggle and deposed deputy minister, now faces a challenge to her leadership of the prominent African National Congress Women's League (ANCWL).
Members will decide on Sunday whether she will retain her post, amid concern in the ruling African National Congress (ANC) over a split in the League which it said compromised its image.
The ANC said on Saturday it was concerned at the lack of unity in the League since a ban on it under apartheid was lifted in 1990.

"The centre of the problem was the fact of disunity which over time...paralysed the effective functioning of the league, weakened the women's movement in general and compromised the image of the ANC considerably," it said in a statement.
The League has enjoyed considerable influence in the ANC, which swept to power under Winnie's former husband Nelson Mandela in South Africa's first all-race elections in 1994.

Its members have included such prominent women as Adelaide Tambo, widow of the late ANC president Oliver Tambo, who quit the League in 1995 in protest at Winnie's style of leadership, which opponents portray as undemocratic.

Madikizela-Mandela, 62, slipped from South Africa's political mainstream when she was sacked from government by President Mandela as deputy arts, culture, science and technology minister in 1995, following her criticism of his unity government. She remains a member of parliament.
An ANC official told Reuters her main opponents for the ANCWL leadership were its current deputy president Thandi Modise and Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma.
Zuma was among 10 ANCWL members who quit its executive committee in 1995 in protest at Madikizela-Mandela's leadership.
Madikizela-Mandela has been shunned by the ANC since the President announced in 1992 that he was separating from her, and following reports of alleged mismanagement of funds under her control.
At the time she resigned from all her ANC posts but was reappointed president of the ANC Women's League in 1993.

Since her divorce from the president last year and reports of financial difficulties, she has kept a low profile, but she still regards herself as the voice of millions of impoverished black South Africans.

As Mandela's wife she endured severe police harassment and was banished in the 1970's to a remote town in the Free State province for her part in the fight for black liberation while her husband was jailed for 27 years.
Her image was scarred by the kidnap and murder of 14-year-old Stompie Seipei in the months before Mandela's release in 1991. Her bodyguard was convicted of the murder.
